WebSocket transport, connection lifecycle and a script-reachable message bus.

## Using it

List it in the top-level `"packages"` array of `project.jengine`:

```json
{
  "packages": [
    { "name": "jengine-net", "source": { "type": "path", "path": "../../packages/jengine-net" } }
  ]
}
```

Then rebuild the editor viewport for the project (`jengine viewport-build projects/<name>`, or the
editor's *Rebuild viewport* banner). Native and web builds link it on their own.

A script can check that the package is linked with `if Net == nil then return end`.

## Script commands

Commands run in every runtime and return nothing; a package publishes what scripts read onto
components (see the notes below). The flat name also works.

| Call | Flat name |
|---|---|
| `Net.connect(url)` | `net_connect` |
| `Net.disconnect()` | `net_disconnect` |
| `Net.send(message)` | `net_send` |
| `Net.http(id, url, method, body)` | `net_http` |

## Notes

*From `packages/jengine-net/README.md`.*

WebSocket transport, HTTP(S) requests, and a message bus game scripts can
reach. **No rooms, no replication, no server** — this is the layer those sit
on, not a replacement for them.

### Opting in

Not linked into the stock runtime, so nothing compiles `tungstenite` unless a
project asks for it. Declare it in `project.jengine`:

```json
{
  "packages": [
    { "name": "jengine-net",
      "source": { "type": "path", "path": "../../packages/jengine-net" } }
  ],
  "settings": { "enabled_packages": ["jengine-physics", "jengine-net"] }
}
```

Then rebuild the viewport so the editor carries it:

```powershell
./build-project-viewport.ps1 -Project projects/my-game
```

`projects/engine-test-lab` is the worked example; scene 66 exercises it.

### Using it from a script

Everything goes through a `Net` custom component on any entity. There are
deliberately **no script globals** — see "The parity constraint" below.

| Field | Written by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `url` | script | server to be connected to; `""` disconnects |
| `outbox` | script | strings to send; the package sends and clears them |
| `inbox` | package | strings received; the script clears them |
| `state` | package | `disconnected` / `connecting` / `connected` / `closed` / `failed` |
| `dropped` | package | messages lost to a full inbox this session |
| `requests` | script | HTTP requests to make; the package clears them |
| `responses` | package | HTTP results; the script clears them |
| `own` | script | `true`: a connection of this entity's own (see below) |

```lua
local net = Entity.find_by_name("Net")

-- Connect. Declarative: state the URL you want, the package reconciles.
Entity.set_custom(net, "Net", "url", "ws://127.0.0.1:2567")

-- Send.
local out = Entity.get_custom(net, "Net", "outbox") or {}
table.insert(out, '{"type":"move","x":3}')
Entity.set_custom(net, "Net", "outbox", out)

-- Receive. The package appends; clearing is yours.
for _, msg in ipairs(Entity.get_custom(net, "Net", "inbox") or {}) do handle(msg) end
Entity.set_custom(net, "Net", "inbox", {})
```

#### HTTP

```lua
-- Queue a request. `id` is how you match the answer back.
local reqs = Entity.get_custom(net, "Net", "requests") or {}
table.insert(reqs, {
  id = "scores", url = "https://api.example.com/scores",
  method = "GET", headers = { ["User-Agent"] = "my-game" },
})
Entity.set_custom(net, "Net", "requests", reqs)

-- Read answers.
for _, r in ipairs(Entity.get_custom(net, "Net", "responses") or {}) do
  if r.error then warn(r.error)        -- never reached a server
  elseif r.ok then use(r.body)         -- 2xx
  else warn(r.status .. ": " .. r.body) -- 404 etc. still carry a body
  end
end
Entity.set_custom(net, "Net", "responses", {})
```

A **status is not a failure**: a 404 is an answer, and its body is usually
where the API explains the problem. Only `error` means the request never
reached a server — DNS, refused, TLS, CORS.

At most 16 requests may be in flight; past that a request is refused *with a
response*, so a script waiting on an id is never left waiting forever.
Response bodies are capped at 8 MB, and are text — a game calling a web API
wants JSON, not a video.

**CORS applies in the browser.** An API that works natively can fail in a web
build for that reason alone, and the browser deliberately will not say why.

`url` is a field rather than a `connect()` call on purpose: a script that
issues commands has to remember whether it already issued one, which goes
wrong the moment a scene reload runs `init()` again against a live connection.

### Using it from Rust

```rust
use jengine_net::{connect, http_client, HttpRequest, NetConnection};

let mut conn = NetConnection::new();
connect(&mut conn, "wss://example.com/game");
conn.pump();                       // once per frame
for msg in conn.drain() { /* … */ }

let mut http = http_client();      // native threads, or `fetch` in a browser
http.send(HttpRequest::get("scores", "https://api.example.com/scores"));
http.pump();                       // once per frame
for r in http.drain() { /* … */ }
```

Rust keeps binary frames; the script channel is text-only, because carrying
bytes through a Lua table means inventing an encoding.

### Using a JS library in a web build (Colyseus, etc.)

Some networking is only practical as JavaScript. Colyseus ships a browser SDK
with its own framing and schema decoding; reimplementing that protocol in Rust
would be a large job permanently chasing upstream, and the SDK is right there.

So the engine binds **no** library. It defines a contract, and a few lines of
JS adapt whichever one you want. Load both through `settings.web_scripts`:

```json
"settings": {
  "web_scripts": [
    "https://unpkg.com/@colyseus/sdk@^0.17.0/dist/colyseus.js",
    "colyseus-adapter.js"
  ]
}
```

The builder emits these as **classic** scripts, in order, ahead of the module
that boots the wasm — the same arrangement `lua-runtime.js` already relies on,
so the library's globals exist before the engine's first frame. A `://` entry
is treated as a URL; anything else is a path under the web root, so you can
vendor a copy instead of depending on a CDN at runtime.

The adapter installs `globalThis.jengineNet` with four methods:

```js
globalThis.jengineNet = {
  connect(url) { return handle; },   // begin connecting
  send(handle, text) {},
  poll(handle) { return events; },   // drain, never peek
  close(handle) {},
};
```

Events are `{type:"open"}`, `{type:"message", data}`,
`{type:"close", code, reason}`, `{type:"error", message}`.

Then connect with a `js:` URL instead of a `ws://` one:

```lua
Entity.set_custom(net, "Net", "url", "js:my_room")     -- default adapter
Entity.set_custom(net, "Net", "url", "js:other:lobby") -- a named adapter
```

Everything after the scheme goes to the adapter untouched, because a library's
addressing is its own business — Colyseus takes a room name where a WebSocket
takes a path. `js:wss://host` is *not* misread as an adapter named `wss`.

A working Colyseus adapter is in `examples/colyseus-adapter.js`.
It is the whole of the coupling, and it is yours to edit.

**This is web-only.** A `js:` URL on native fails with a message saying so,
rather than handing `js:...` to a DNS resolver. A game that wants the same
protocol in a native build needs a Rust client for it.

### The parity constraint

A package *can* register real script functions, but `install_script_api` is
wired only into `ScriptSystem` — the native Luau and QuickJS bridges. The
editor viewport and web runtime execute Lua through Fengari against a
hardcoded `BRIDGE_FUNCTIONS` allowlist that knows nothing about packages, so a
`Net.send()` global would be `nil` in the runtime this engine is developed in.

`Entity.get_custom` / `Entity.set_custom` are core bridge functions present in all four
runtimes, so the channel above behaves identically everywhere. If package
script APIs are ever installed by the browser hosts, a global wrapper becomes
worth adding — until then it would be a trap.

Every `Net` component shares **one** connection, mirrored to all of them:
`url` on any of them connects it, `inbox` and `state` are the same on each.
A component with `own: true` gets a connection **of its own** instead - its
`url`, its `outbox`, its `inbox` - which is what a scene with two sessions
(a split screen, two servers) needs; `jengine-online` sets it on its entity.

### What is deliberately missing

- **Reconnection.** A failed connection stays failed until the `url` changes.
  A silent reconnect would replay game state the caller never asked to resend.
- **A server.** This is a client; in a browser it could not be anything else.
- **Replication.** No entity sync, authority, or interest management here:
  that is `jengine-online` (a pool of `online_slot`s shown from a
  `jengine-server` room's `sync` frames). `NetworkIdentity` used to be carried
  for it and was read by nothing; it is gone.

### Building on it

Both a Colyseus client and a hand-rolled protocol are *users* of `Transport`,
not replacements for it: both speak WebSocket underneath. Implement your
protocol over `NetConnection`, or over `Transport` directly if you need to
frame messages yourself. `MockTransport` lets the whole thing be tested
without a socket — every test in this package works that way.
